stem: In LangChain terms, what is the core difference between a chain and an agent?

options.text: In a chain the code fixes the steps; in an agent the model picks them at runtime
options.why: That is the distinction interviewers want: control flow is fixed in code for a chain and model-driven for an agent.

options.text: A chain can call only one model, while an agent can call several different models in parallel
options.why: Chains can call several models; the number of models is not what separates the two.

options.text: Agents are always faster and cheaper because they skip unnecessary steps
options.why: Agents usually cost more and are less predictable, because every loop iteration is another model call.

options.text: A chain cannot use tools at all, while an agent must use at least one tool
options.why: A fixed pipeline can call a tool as one of its steps, and an agent with no tool calls simply answers directly.

explanation: A chain (or workflow) is a predetermined sequence: retrieve, then prompt, then parse. An agent puts a model in a loop where it picks tools and decides when it is done. Pick a chain when the steps are known in advance and you need predictability; pick an agent when the path depends on what the model learns along the way.

stem: In a `create_agent` run with no middleware, the loop ends when the model returns an `AIMessage` that contains no tool calls.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: a model reply without tool calls is the normal stop condition, and that reply becomes the final message.

options.text: False
options.why: Without middleware or a limit, nothing else ends the loop; the model signals it is done by not requesting a tool.

explanation: The agent alternates between the model node and the tools node. Each tool call produces a `ToolMessage` that goes back to the model. When the model answers without requesting any tool, the run finishes. Middleware jumps, call limits, `return_direct` tools and the recursion limit are the other ways a run can end.

stem: In LangChain 1.x, which import gives you the standard prebuilt tool-calling agent?

options.text: `from langchain.agents import create_agent`
options.why: This is the 1.x entry point; it replaces LangGraph's `create_react_agent` and the old `AgentExecutor` setups.

options.text: `from langchain.agents import AgentExecutor`
options.why: `AgentExecutor` is no longer in `langchain.agents` in 1.x; this import raises `ImportError`. It lives on in `langchain-classic`.

options.text: `from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent`
options.why: This still imports, but it is deprecated and points you to `langchain.agents.create_agent`.

options.text: `from langchain.agents import initialize_agent`
options.why: `initialize_agent` is a legacy helper that now lives only in `langchain_classic.agents`.

explanation: LangChain 1.x consolidated agents into `create_agent`, which returns a compiled LangGraph graph. Legacy APIs such as `AgentExecutor` and `initialize_agent` moved to the `langchain-classic` package, and `langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent` emits a deprecation warning that names the new import.

stem: You call `create_agent(..., response_format=Answer)` and then `result = agent.invoke(...)`. Under which key of `result` do you find the validated `Answer` object? Type the key name.
explanation: The structured result is stored in the agent state under `structured_response`, separate from `messages`. Reading the last message's text instead gives you the tool-message summary or free text, not the validated object.

stem: When an agent decides which tool to call, what information about each tool does the model actually use?

options.text: Its name, description (the docstring) and argument schema
options.why: These are sent to the model with the request, so a vague docstring or name leads to wrong tool choices.

options.text: The source code of the tool's function body
options.why: The function body never leaves your process; the model sees only the schema.

options.text: The order in which tools appear in the list, since it always tries the first one
options.why: The model chooses by relevance to the conversation, not by list position.

options.text: Past execution times of each tool, stored by LangChain
options.why: LangChain does not send timing statistics to the model.

explanation: Tool calling works on schemas: the model receives each tool's name, description and input schema and returns a structured call with arguments. This is why good docstrings and precise type hints matter so much. The body of the function runs only when the agent executes the call.

stem: Match each production problem with the built-in middleware that addresses it.

options.text: `SummarizationMiddleware`
options.why: Condenses older messages once a size threshold is reached.

options.text: `ModelCallLimitMiddleware`
options.why: Caps how many model calls a run or thread may make.

options.text: `ModelFallbackMiddleware`
options.why: Tries alternative models when the primary model call fails.

options.text: `PIIMiddleware`
options.why: Detects personal data and redacts, masks, hashes or blocks it.

prompts.text: A long-running support chat is approaching the model's context window
A buggy prompt makes the agent call the model dozens of times per request
The primary model provider is returning errors during an outage
Customer email addresses must not be sent to the model

explanation: A long support chat creeps toward the context window limit. Summarization replaces old history with a summary. A runaway agent burns money in a loop: a model call limit stops it. A provider outage takes down your primary model: a fallback chain moves to the next model. Customer emails must not reach the model: PII middleware rewrites or blocks them.

stem: How do you give a `create_agent` agent a fixed system prompt in LangChain 1.x?

options.text: Pass `system_prompt="..."` to `create_agent`
options.why: `system_prompt` accepts a string or a `SystemMessage` and is applied to every model call.

options.text: Pass `prompt="..."` to `create_agent`
options.why: `prompt` was the parameter name on LangGraph's `create_react_agent`; it was renamed to `system_prompt`.

options.text: Add a `SystemMessage` to the `tools` list
options.why: The `tools` list holds tools only; a message there is not a valid tool.

options.text: Set `config={"configurable": {"system": "..."}}` on every invoke
options.why: There is no such configurable key; the system prompt is set on the agent or by middleware.

explanation: `system_prompt` is the static instruction for every model call. It is not stored in the `messages` state; the agent prepends it at call time. When the prompt must vary per request, use dynamic prompt middleware rather than rebuilding the agent.

stem: Which of these middleware hooks are node-style hooks, running at fixed points and returning a state update (or `None`)? (Choose three.)

options.text: `before_agent`
options.why: Node-style: runs once at the start of each invocation.

options.text: `before_model`
options.why: Node-style: runs before each model call and can return a state update.

options.text: `after_model`
options.why: Node-style: runs after each model response.

options.text: `wrap_model_call`
options.why: Wrap-style: it receives a `handler` and decides whether and how to call the model.

options.text: `wrap_tool_call`
options.why: Wrap-style: it wraps each tool execution and can retry, short-circuit or convert errors.

explanation: Middleware has two hook families. Node-style hooks (`before_agent`, `before_model`, `after_model`, `after_agent`) run as graph nodes and return dict updates that merge into state. Wrap-style hooks (`wrap_model_call`, `wrap_tool_call`) surround each call and control the handler, which is how retries, caching and request rewriting are built.

stem: An agent has one middleware that implements every hook. The model calls one tool, then answers. Order the hooks by when each first runs.

options.text: `before_agent`
`before_model`
`wrap_model_call`
`after_model`
`wrap_tool_call`
`after_agent`

explanation: `before_agent` runs once at the start. Each model step is `before_model`, then `wrap_model_call` around the actual call, then `after_model`. The tool call then runs inside `wrap_tool_call`. After the second model step (which repeats `before_model`, `wrap_model_call` and `after_model`), `after_agent` runs once at the end. Running a stub agent with a fake model and logging hooks confirms this order.

stem: An agent uses `ModelCallLimitMiddleware(run_limit=3)` with no other options. A prompt bug makes the model request a tool on every turn. What happens on the run?

options.text: The run raises `ModelCallLimitExceededError` on the fourth model call
options.why: That happens only with `exit_behavior="error"`; the default is `"end"`.

options.text: It stops after three model calls and returns normally with a limit notice
options.why: The default `exit_behavior` is `"end"`, which ends the run gracefully instead of raising.

options.text: Nothing changes, because `run_limit` only counts calls across a whole thread
options.why: That describes `thread_limit`; `run_limit` counts calls within one invocation.

options.text: The middleware silently drops tool calls but keeps calling the model
options.why: That resembles `ToolCallLimitMiddleware`'s `continue` behaviour, not the model call limit.

explanation: `ModelCallLimitMiddleware` supports `run_limit` (per invocation) and `thread_limit` (across invocations on a thread, which needs a checkpointer). With the default `exit_behavior="end"`, the agent stops and appends a message such as "Model call limits exceeded: run limit (3/3)". Use `"error"` when the caller must treat the cutoff as a failure.

stem: You are migrating a legacy agent to LangChain 1.x. Match each old setting with its closest 1.x equivalent.

options.text: A checkpointer on `create_agent` plus a `thread_id` in the config
options.why: Persists the agent's message state per conversation.

options.text: `ModelCallLimitMiddleware` with a `run_limit`
options.why: Caps model calls in one invocation.

options.text: The `system_prompt` parameter
options.why: Static instructions applied to every model call.

options.text: A middleware with a `before_model` hook
options.why: Custom logic that runs before every model call.

explanation: Memory classes attached to `AgentExecutor` become short-term memory via a checkpointer and `thread_id`. An iteration cap maps most closely to call-limit middleware (the graph's recursion limit is a cruder safety net that raises an error). `create_react_agent(prompt=...)` became `create_agent(system_prompt=...)`, and `pre_model_hook` became a `before_model` middleware hook.

stem: The model calls `add(a, b)` (both `int`) with arguments `{"a": "x"}`. With a plain `create_agent` and no middleware, what happens?

options.text: The agent raises a Pydantic `ValidationError` and the run fails
options.why: Argument validation failures are caught by the tool node instead of crashing the run.

options.text: The tool runs with `a` coerced to 0 and `b` defaulted to 0
options.why: Nothing is coerced or defaulted; the call is rejected before the tool body runs.

options.text: An error `ToolMessage` goes back to the model so it can fix the call
options.why: Invalid arguments become a `ToolMessage` with `status="error"` that asks the model to fix the call.

options.text: The agent skips the call and returns the model's empty message as the final answer
options.why: The loop continues; the error message is fed back to the model.

explanation: Schema validation of tool arguments happens before the tool body. When it fails, the agent returns an error `ToolMessage` (in the version tested, it lists the bad fields and ends with "Please fix the error and try again"), so the model gets another chance. This differs from an exception raised inside the tool body, which is not caught by default.

stem: If you add `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware` to `create_agent` without a checkpointer, `create_agent` raises an error immediately.

options.text: True
options.why: No error is raised at build time; the agent can even pause. The failure shows up when you try to resume.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the graph builds and can pause, but `Command(resume=...)` then fails with "Cannot use Command(resume=...) without checkpointer".

explanation: Human-in-the-loop works by interrupting the graph and saving its state, so the run can continue later. Without a checkpointer there is nothing to resume from: the first call returns an interrupt, and the resume call raises a `RuntimeError`. Configure a checkpointer (a persistent one in production) and pass the same `thread_id` on both calls.

stem: Each request comes from a logged-in user, and one tool needs the user's id. The id must not be visible to or chosen by the model. Which approach fits `create_agent`?

options.text: Put the user id in the system prompt and ask the model to pass it as a tool argument
options.why: The model could alter or leak the id, and it ends up in the prompt.

options.text: Set `context_schema`, pass `context=` on `invoke`, read it via `ToolRuntime` in the tool
options.why: Runtime context is dependency injection: the `runtime` parameter is hidden from the model's tool schema.

options.text: Store the user id in a module-level global set by the API handler before each `invoke` call
options.why: Globals race across concurrent requests and leak between users.

options.text: Rebuild the agent on every request, baking the id into each tool through a closure
options.why: That works, but it is wasteful and unnecessary when context injection exists.

explanation: `context_schema` types the per-invocation context, `invoke(..., context=...)` supplies it, and tools read it through a `ToolRuntime` parameter that never appears in the schema sent to the model. Middleware reads the same data via `runtime.context` (node-style hooks) or `request.runtime.context` (wrap-style hooks).

stem: An agent is built with `system_prompt="static"` and a `@dynamic_prompt` middleware that returns `f"user is {request.runtime.context['name']}"`. What system prompt does the model receive?

options.text: "static" followed by "user is ..." as two system messages
options.why: The dynamic prompt does not add a second system message.

options.text: Only "static", because `system_prompt` always takes priority
options.why: Middleware runs at call time and overrides the static value.

options.text: Only the dynamically generated "user is ..." text
options.why: The function's return value replaces the system message for that model call.

options.text: Neither: combining the two raises a configuration error
options.why: The combination is allowed; the static prompt is simply replaced.

explanation: `@dynamic_prompt` wraps a function that receives the `ModelRequest` and returns the system prompt for that call. A run with a fake model and a spy middleware shows the request's system prompt is exactly the generated string. If you want to keep the static text, read `request.system_prompt` inside the function and build on it.

stem: Which decorator from `langchain.agents.middleware` turns a function that returns a string into middleware that sets the system prompt for each model call? Type the decorator name.
explanation: `@dynamic_prompt` is a shortcut for a `wrap_model_call` that replaces the system message. Use it when the prompt depends on runtime context or state, such as the user's role or language.

stem: Older LangChain agents used ReAct-style prompting, where the model wrote "Thought / Action / Action Input" text that was parsed with regexes. Why did LangChain move to native tool-calling agents?

options.text: Providers return structured tool calls, so no fragile text parsing is needed
options.why: That is the main gain: `AIMessage.tool_calls` arrives already structured, so there are no output-parsing errors on format drift.

options.text: ReAct prompting cannot use more than one tool in a run
options.why: ReAct agents could use many tools; the weakness was parsing reliability, not tool count.

options.text: Native tool calling removes the need for any loop, since the provider runs the tools
options.why: The provider only proposes calls; your agent still executes tools and loops.

options.text: ReAct agents cannot reason step by step
options.why: Step-by-step reasoning was ReAct's whole point; it was the text format that was brittle.

explanation: ReAct's thought, action and observation cycle survives as an idea, but modern models emit structured `tool_calls` through the provider API. That removes `handle_parsing_errors`-style failures and allows parallel calls. Interviewers often ask for this trade-off: less prompt engineering of formats, and dependence on models that support tool calling.

stem: With `PIIMiddleware("email", strategy=...)` on user input, which strategies let the request continue to the model with the email altered? (Choose three.)

options.text: `"redact"`
options.why: Replaces the email with a placeholder such as `[REDACTED_EMAIL]`.

options.text: `"mask"`
options.why: Keeps part of the value and stars out the rest, for example `asha@****.com`.

options.text: `"hash"`
options.why: Replaces the value with a deterministic hash token, so equal emails stay linkable.

options.text: `"block"`
options.why: Blocking raises `PIIDetectionError`, so the request does not continue.

options.text: `"encrypt"`
options.why: There is no encrypt strategy; the options are block, redact, mask and hash.

explanation: `redact` removes the value, `mask` hides most of it, and `hash` swaps in a stable token so you can still join records without seeing the raw value. `block` stops the run with an exception. The default strategy is `redact`, and by default only user input is checked.

stem: Which values are valid `jump_to` targets for a middleware hook that declares them in `can_jump_to`? (Choose three.)

options.text: `"end"`
options.why: Ends the run, passing through any `after_agent` hooks.

options.text: `"model"`
options.why: Goes back to the model step, starting at the first `before_model` hook.

options.text: `"tools"`
options.why: Goes to the tool-execution node.

options.text: `"start"`
options.why: There is no start target; restart logic would jump to the model.

options.text: `"before_agent"`
options.why: Hook names are not jump targets, and `before_agent` runs only once per invocation.

explanation: A node-style hook can return `{"jump_to": ...}` alongside its state update. The three targets are `end`, `model` and `tools`, and each must be declared in `can_jump_to` with `@hook_config(...)` on a class method or the `can_jump_to=` argument of a decorator.

stem: A tool's body raises `ValueError("kaboom")`. The agent is a plain `create_agent` with no middleware. What happens?

options.text: The model receives an error `ToolMessage` saying "kaboom" and can try again
options.why: That is what happens for invalid arguments, or once you add error-handling middleware; an exception from the tool body is not caught by default.

options.text: The `ValueError` propagates out of `invoke` and the run fails
options.why: By default, exceptions raised inside the tool body are re-raised. Catch them with `wrap_tool_call`, `ToolRetryMiddleware` or `ToolErrorMiddleware`.

options.text: The tool is retried twice with exponential backoff before failing
options.why: Retries happen only with `ToolRetryMiddleware`.

options.text: The agent silently drops the tool call and ends with the model's previous message
options.why: Errors are never silently swallowed.

explanation: Validation errors (bad arguments) and unknown tool names are turned into error `ToolMessage`s, but exceptions from the tool's own code propagate in the default setup, which was confirmed by running it. For production, add a `wrap_tool_call` that converts exceptions to a readable `ToolMessage(status="error")`, or use the built-in retry and error middleware, so the model can recover.

stem: Three middleware are passed as `middleware=[m1, m2, m3]`, each with an `after_model` hook. In what order do those hooks run after a model call?

options.why: That is the order for `before_model`; after-hooks are reversed.
After-hooks unwind in reverse, mirroring the nesting of wrap hooks.

options.text: All three run concurrently, in no guaranteed order
options.why: Hooks run sequentially as graph nodes, in a defined order.

options.text: Only m1's hook runs, because the first middleware wins
options.why: Every registered hook runs.

explanation: Think of the list as layers around the model: `before_*` hooks run first to last, `wrap_*` hooks nest with the first middleware outermost, and `after_*` hooks run last to first. The same rule applies to `before_agent` and `after_agent`.

stem: An agent pauses on `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={"refund": True})` with `InMemorySaver` and `config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "t1"}}`. The reviewer approves. How do you continue the run?

options.text: Call `agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "approved"}]}, config)`
options.why: A new user message starts a new turn; the pending tool call is still waiting for a decision.

options.text: Call `agent.invoke(Command(resume={"decisions": [{"type": "approve"}]}), config)` with the same thread id
options.why: Resuming with a `Command` that carries one decision per pending action continues the paused run.

options.text: Call `agent.invoke(Command(resume={"decisions": [{"type": "approve"}]}))` with no config, since the saver remembers the last run
options.why: Without the thread id, the checkpointer cannot locate the paused state.

options.text: Call the `refund` tool yourself and append the `ToolMessage` to state
options.why: Bypassing the middleware loses the audit trail and leaves the interrupt pending.

explanation: The interrupt's value lists `action_requests` (name, args, description) and `review_configs` (allowed decisions). Resume with `Command(resume={"decisions": [...]})` on the same `thread_id`, giving one decision per action in the same order. Approve runs the call; edit runs it with new arguments; reject skips it and sends feedback to the model.

stem: A reviewer decides a proposed `refund` call must not happen, and the model should be told why. Which decision should the resume payload use?

options.text: `{"type": "respond", "message": "Refunds over 5000 need a manager"}`
options.why: `respond` returns the message as a successful tool result, so the model may believe the refund happened.

options.text: `{"type": "edit", "edited_action": {"name": "refund", "args": {"order_id": ""}}}`
options.why: Editing still executes the tool, now with empty arguments.

options.text: `{"type": "reject", "message": "Refunds over 5000 need a manager"}`
options.why: Reject skips the call and feeds the reason back to the model as the tool result.

options.text: `{"type": "approve", "message": "denied"}`
options.why: Approve runs the tool regardless of any message.

explanation: `reject` is the deny decision: the tool does not run and the model gets a message explaining the rejection, so it can tell the user or choose another path. The docs reserve `respond` for cases where the human is acting as the tool (for example answering an `ask_user` question), because the model reads it as a successful result.

stem: With `response_format=ToolStrategy(Answer)`, the model returns `{"city": "Pune", "temp": "hot"}` where `temp: int`. What happens with the default settings?

options.text: The agent raises `StructuredOutputValidationError` immediately
options.why: That happens only with `handle_errors=False`.

options.text: `structured_response` is set to `None` and the run ends
options.why: The agent does not quietly give up on the first invalid output.

options.text: The agent stores the raw dict in `structured_response` without validation
options.why: Validation against the schema is the point of the strategy.

options.text: The error is sent back as a `ToolMessage` and the model retries
options.why: `handle_errors` defaults to `True`, which retries with feedback ending in "Please fix your mistakes."

explanation: `ToolStrategy` exposes the schema as an artificial tool. When the model's arguments fail validation, the default `handle_errors=True` feeds the error back as a `ToolMessage` so the model can correct itself. You can pass a fixed string, a set of exception types or a callable to customise this, or `False` to raise instead.

stem: You want the model to see only the last 10 messages on each call, but the checkpointer must keep the full conversation for auditing. Which implementation meets both requirements?

options.text: A `before_model` hook that returns `{"messages": state["messages"][-10:]}`
options.why: Returned messages are merged into state by the reducer, which appends them, so this duplicates messages instead of trimming.

options.text: A `wrap_model_call` that calls `handler(request.override(messages=request.messages[-10:]))`
options.why: The override changes only what this model call sees; the state, and so the checkpoint, keeps everything.

options.text: A `before_model` hook that removes all messages with `RemoveMessage` and re-adds the last 10
options.why: This trims, but it permanently deletes history from state, which breaks the audit requirement.

options.text: Setting `recursion_limit=10` in the config
options.why: The recursion limit caps graph steps; it does not trim context.

explanation: There are two places to manage context. State updates from node-style hooks are permanent. Request overrides in `wrap_model_call` are per call and leave state untouched. A test agent that overrides messages to the last one still returns the full history in the final state.

stem: A team adds `SummarizationMiddleware(model="anthropic:claude-haiku-5-5")` to a chat agent. Weeks later, long threads still hit context-length errors and no summaries ever appear. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The summarization model must be the same model instance as the agent's main model
options.why: A cheaper summarizer model is a common, supported choice.

options.text: No `trigger` was configured, so summarization never fires automatically
options.why: `trigger` has no default; without one the middleware never decides to summarize.

options.text: `keep` defaults to 0 messages, so every summary is discarded
options.why: `keep` defaults to keeping the 20 most recent messages.

options.text: Summarization runs only when a checkpointer is absent
options.why: Summarization works with or without a checkpointer.

explanation: `trigger` takes thresholds such as `("tokens", 4000)`, `("messages", 50)` or `("fraction", 0.8)`, or combinations of them, and `keep` decides how much recent context survives unsummarized. Summaries keep the meaning of older turns, but lose exact wording and cost an extra model call each time they fire.

stem: You want a cheap model for short conversations and a stronger model once a conversation has more than 10 messages. What is the recommended way to do this with `create_agent` in 1.x?

options.text: Pass a callable as `model=` that picks a model from the state
options.why: Callable models were the old dynamic-model approach and moved to middleware in 1.x.

options.text: Create two agents and pick one in your API handler for each request
options.why: This works, but it cannot switch mid-run and duplicates configuration.

options.text: A `wrap_model_call` middleware that calls `handler(request.override(model=...))`, choosing the model from `request.messages`
options.why: Middleware sees the live request and can swap the model on every call, even mid-run.

options.text: Use `init_chat_model` with `configurable_fields` and change the model through `config` from inside a tool
options.why: Tools cannot reconfigure the model used for the current call.

explanation: The v1 migration moved dynamic model selection into `wrap_model_call`. Because it runs before every model call, it can pick by message count, runtime context (such as the user's plan) or state, and the decision applies inside a single run as the conversation grows.

stem: Which statements about `ToolCallLimitMiddleware` are correct? (Choose three.)

options.text: Its default `exit_behavior` is `"continue"`: calls over the limit are blocked with error `ToolMessage`s, and the model keeps running
options.why: Blocked calls get a message such as "Tool call limit exceeded", and the loop continues.

options.text: Constructing it without `run_limit` or `thread_limit` raises a `ValueError`
options.why: At least one limit must be set.

options.text: `thread_limit` counts calls across invocations, so it needs a checkpointer to persist the count
options.why: Thread-level counts live in persisted state.

options.text: It limits model calls, so it replaces `ModelCallLimitMiddleware`
options.why: It counts tool calls only; the two limits are complementary.

options.text: With default settings, the run raises `ToolCallLimitExceededError` once the limit is hit
options.why: Raising requires `exit_behavior="error"`.

explanation: Tool call limits can be global or per tool (`tool_name=`). With `continue`, the model may keep asking for the blocked tool, so pair the limit with a model call limit or choose `end` or `error` when a hard stop is needed.

stem: In a single `invoke` where the model is called three times, a middleware's `before_agent` hook runs once, while its `before_model` hook runs three times.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: agent-level hooks run once per invocation, and model-level hooks run around every model call.

options.text: False
options.why: `before_agent` does not repeat for each loop iteration; that is what `before_model` is for.

explanation: Use `before_agent` for once-per-request work such as loading a user profile or validating input, and `before_model` for per-call work such as trimming or injecting fresh context. `after_agent` likewise runs once at the end. A counting test with a fake model confirms this.

stem: Order the steps of a human-approved tool call with `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware` and a checkpointer.

options.text: The model returns an `AIMessage` with a tool call to a gated tool
The middleware raises an interrupt, and the checkpointer saves the paused state
Your app reads the interrupt's `action_requests` and shows them to a reviewer
Your app invokes the agent with `Command(resume={"decisions": [...]})` on the same `thread_id`
The tool runs (or is skipped on reject) and its `ToolMessage` returns to the model

explanation: Approval happens after the model proposes a call and before the tool executes. The paused state lives in the checkpointer, keyed by thread id, so the resume can happen in a different process minutes or days later. A test run shows the state holds only the human and AI messages until the resume adds the `ToolMessage`.

stem: An agent has `ModelCallLimitMiddleware(thread_limit=2)` (default exit behaviour) and a checkpointer. A user sends three messages on one thread, and each needs exactly one model call. On which message number does the reply become the limit notice instead of a model answer? Type a number.
explanation: `thread_limit` counts model calls across every invocation on the thread, so turns one and two use the budget, and the third turn ends immediately with a message such as "Model call limits exceeded: thread limit (2/2)". `run_limit` would reset on every invoke.

stem: With `response_format=ToolStrategy(Answer)`, the model first returns invalid arguments for `Answer`, then valid ones. Order the messages as they appear in the final `messages` state.

options.text: `HumanMessage` with the user's question
`AIMessage` calling the `Answer` tool with invalid arguments
`ToolMessage` describing the validation error
`AIMessage` calling the `Answer` tool with valid arguments
`ToolMessage` confirming the returned structured response

explanation: Structured output in 1.x is generated inside the main loop: the schema is a tool, failures produce an error `ToolMessage`, and success adds a confirming `ToolMessage` and fills `structured_response`. Running this with a fake model gives exactly this sequence.

stem: Which of these end a `create_agent` run without raising an exception? (Choose three.)

options.text: The model replies with no tool calls
options.why: This is the normal stop condition.

options.text: The model calls a tool defined with `@tool(return_direct=True)`
options.why: The tool's output becomes the final message, and the model is not called again.

options.text: `ModelCallLimitMiddleware(run_limit=3)` reaches its limit
options.why: The default `exit_behavior="end"` stops the run gracefully.

options.text: `ToolCallLimitMiddleware(run_limit=2)` is exceeded with default settings
options.why: The default `continue` blocks extra tool calls but lets the model keep running.

options.text: The model sends invalid tool arguments
options.why: This produces an error `ToolMessage`, and the loop continues.

explanation: Interviewers like the stopping question because several mechanisms exist. Normal completion, `return_direct` tools, graceful limits and `jump_to: "end"` all finish cleanly. Recursion-limit hits and `exit_behavior="error"` raise. Error tool messages and `continue` limits keep the loop going.

stem: Match each requirement with the middleware hook best suited to it.

options.text: `wrap_tool_call`
options.why: Surrounds each tool execution.

options.text: `wrap_model_call`
options.why: Surrounds each model call and can rewrite the request.

options.text: `before_agent`
options.why: Runs once at the start of an invocation.

options.text: `after_model`
options.why: Runs after each model response and can jump.

prompts.text: Convert exceptions raised by tools into readable error messages for the model
Switch to a larger model when the conversation gets long
Load the user's profile into state once per request
Check each model reply against a policy and send the model back to retry if it fails

explanation: Pick the hook by scope and power. Wrap hooks control the call itself (retry, convert errors, swap model or tools). `before_agent` is once per request. `after_model` sees each response and can jump back to the model or to the end.

stem: Middleware is `[Retry(), Logger(), Flaky()]`, all wrap-style. `Retry.wrap_model_call` catches an exception from `handler` and calls `handler` once more. `Logger` logs on entry. `Flaky` raises on its first call only. How many log lines does one model step produce, and what happens if you swap to `[Logger(), Retry(), Flaky()]`?

options.text: 2 with Retry first, 1 with Logger first
options.why: Retry's handler includes Logger, so a retry re-enters it; with Logger outermost, it runs once around the whole retry.

options.text: 1 in both orders, since logging happens only once per model call
options.why: Wrap hooks nest; any middleware inside the retry wrapper runs again on each attempt.

options.text: 2 in both orders, since every attempt passes through every middleware
options.why: When Logger is outside Retry, the retry happens below it and Logger sees one call.

options.text: 1 with Retry first, 2 with Logger first
options.why: This reverses the nesting: the first middleware is the outermost layer.

explanation: In `wrap_model_call`, the first middleware is outermost, and `handler` is the rest of the stack. A test with both orders confirms 2 and 1 log lines. Put metering or audit logging outside retries if you want one entry per logical call, or inside if you want every attempt counted.

options.text: `before_model` hooks may only return `jump_to`, never new messages, so the update is rejected
options.why: Node hooks can return any state update, including messages.

options.text: `jump_to` only works from `after_model` hooks
options.why: `before_model`, `after_model` and the agent-level hooks can all jump.

options.text: `can_jump_to=["end"]` was not declared, so the jump is ignored
options.why: Without the declaration, the message is added but the jump has no effect; `@before_model(can_jump_to=["end"])` fixes it.

options.text: `"end"` is not a valid target; it should be `"__end__"`
options.why: The public target names are `end`, `model` and `tools`.

explanation: Jump targets must be declared so the graph wires the conditional edges. In the version tested, an undeclared jump fails silently: the state shows "Request blocked." followed by the model's answer. Declaring `can_jump_to` makes the run stop right after the hook. This is a classic code-review catch.

stem: Which statements about `response_format` in `create_agent` are correct? (Choose three.)

options.text: Passing a Pydantic class directly uses `ProviderStrategy` if the model's profile reports native structured output, and `ToolStrategy` otherwise
options.why: Auto-selection reads model profile data and falls back to tool calling.

options.text: A raw JSON Schema dict must be wrapped in `ToolStrategy` or `ProviderStrategy`
options.why: Dicts are not auto-detected as schemas.

options.text: Union types such as `A | B` are supported with `ToolStrategy`, and the model picks which schema to fill
options.why: Each union member becomes its own output tool.

options.text: The 0.x-style tuple `("prompt text", Schema)` still enables prompted structured output
options.why: Prompted output was removed in 1.x.

options.text: Structured output runs as a separate node after the agent finishes, with one extra model call
options.why: In 1.x it is produced inside the main loop, not by a trailing node.

explanation: Choose `ProviderStrategy` for provider-enforced schemas (with optional `strict`). Choose `ToolStrategy` for any tool-calling model, for unions, and for retry-on-error behaviour. The validated result lands in `structured_response`.

stem: A `wrap_model_call` middleware adds an MCP-discovered tool to `request.tools`, but the tool was never passed to `create_agent`. The model calls it. What happens, and what is the fix?

options.text: The tool runs normally, since the model's request included it
options.why: The tool node can only execute tools it knows about.

options.text: The agent returns an error `ToolMessage` saying the tool does not exist, and continues
options.why: That is the behaviour for a hallucinated name; middleware-added tools fail more loudly.

options.text: The agent raises a `ValueError` about middleware adding unknown tools; register the tool on the agent, or add a `wrap_tool_call` that executes it
options.why: The tool node rejects unregistered tools, and the docs say runtime-registered tools need `wrap_tool_call` to run.

options.text: The agent silently removes the tool from the request before calling the model
options.why: The request is sent as modified; the failure comes at execution.

explanation: Filtering registered tools in `wrap_model_call` is safe and common (permissions, relevance). Adding new tools there changes only what the model sees, so the execution side must know them too: register them up front, or pair the change with `wrap_tool_call` that handles those calls. A test raised "Middleware added tools that the agent doesn't know how to execute".

stem: A custom middleware class implements only `wrap_model_call` (sync). The team deploys the agent behind an async FastAPI endpoint using `await agent.ainvoke(...)`. What happens?

options.text: It works, because LangChain automatically runs the sync hook in a worker thread pool
options.why: That fallback applies to node-style hooks such as `before_model`, not to wrap-style hooks.

options.text: The hook is skipped in async mode, and the model is called directly
options.why: Hooks are never silently skipped.

options.text: The agent deadlocks waiting for the sync handler
options.why: It fails fast with a clear error instead.

options.text: It raises `NotImplementedError`: the async `awrap_model_call` is missing
options.why: Wrap-style hooks need an async implementation when the agent runs asynchronously.

explanation: Node-style hooks defined only as sync still run under `ainvoke`. Wrap-style hooks must match the execution mode: sync-only fails under `ainvoke`, and async-only (`awrap_model_call`) fails under `invoke`. Class-based middleware that defines both is the recommended pattern for reusable middleware, which is one reason to prefer classes over decorators.

stem: An agent must stop after 10 model calls per request and 50 per conversation thread. A developer writes `middleware=[ModelCallLimitMiddleware(run_limit=10), ModelCallLimitMiddleware(thread_limit=50)]`. What happens, and what is the better design?

options.text: Both limits apply independently; this is the intended pattern
options.why: Two instances of the same middleware class are rejected when the agent is built.

options.text: `create_agent` fails with an assertion about duplicate middleware; use one `ModelCallLimitMiddleware(run_limit=10, thread_limit=50)` with a checkpointer
options.why: Middleware instances of the same class collide by name, and one instance supports both limits.

options.text: Only the last instance applies, since later middleware overrides earlier ones
options.why: Nothing is silently overridden; the build fails.

options.text: Only the first instance applies, and the thread limit is ignored without a warning
options.why: The build fails before any limit can apply.

explanation: Middleware get node names from their class name, so two instances of one class collide (the build fails with "Please remove duplicate middleware instances"). One call-limit middleware takes both `run_limit` and `thread_limit`. The thread count needs a checkpointer and a `thread_id` to persist across requests.

stem: `PIIMiddleware("email")` is installed with default options. A tool returns a customer record containing an email, and the model repeats that email in its final answer. Why did nothing get redacted, and what fixes it?

options.text: Only `strategy="block"` inspects tool results; switch the strategy
options.why: The strategy decides what happens on a match; the `apply_to_*` flags decide where to look.

options.text: PII middleware runs only in async agents
options.why: It works in sync runs; the test used `invoke`.

options.text: The email regex does not match addresses inside JSON
options.why: Detection worked once the right flags were enabled.

options.text: By default only user input is checked; set `apply_to_tool_results=True` and `apply_to_output=True`
options.why: Both flags default to `False`, so tool outputs and AI replies pass through untouched.

explanation: `apply_to_input` defaults to `True`, while `apply_to_output` and `apply_to_tool_results` default to `False`. Turning both on redacted the email in the `ToolMessage` the model saw and in the final reply. Data that enters through tools is a common leak path.

stem: You are migrating an `AgentExecutor` agent with memory, custom error handling and a Pydantic state model to LangChain 1.x. Which statements are correct? (Choose three.)

options.text: `AgentExecutor` and `initialize_agent` remain available only through the `langchain-classic` package
options.why: They moved out of `langchain` in 1.x, so you can migrate gradually.

options.text: Conversation memory becomes a checkpointer on `create_agent` plus a `thread_id` per conversation
options.why: Short-term memory is persisted graph state.

options.text: Custom tool error handling moves into a `wrap_tool_call` middleware
options.why: The v1 guide replaces `handle_tool_errors` with `wrap_tool_call`.

options.text: You can keep the Pydantic model as `state_schema`, since `create_agent` validates it on every step
options.why: `create_agent` supports only `TypedDict` state extending `AgentState`; move validation into middleware.

options.text: Per-request data such as `user_id` must still go through `config["configurable"]`
options.why: 1.x prefers `context=` with `context_schema`; the old pattern works but is not required.

explanation: A safe migration runs the old and new agents side by side on the same eval set (LangSmith helps), maps iteration caps to call limits, moves memory to checkpointers, and turns hooks and error handling into middleware.

stem: In a take-home, you build a customer-support agent for an online music store with tools `lookup_order`, `search_catalog`, `update_email` and `issue_refund`. Reviewers ask how you prevent costly mistakes without slowing down routine queries. Which design best answers that?

options.text: Gate every tool with `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware` so a human approves each call
options.why: Gating read-only lookups adds latency and reviewer fatigue for no safety gain.

options.text: Add a system prompt telling the model never to refund more than a set amount
options.why: Prompt instructions are not enforcement; a jailbreak or a model mistake bypasses them.

options.text: Gate only `issue_refund` and `update_email` with `interrupt_on`, set the read-only tools to `False`, and add a checkpointer and `thread_id` so paused runs can resume
options.why: Approval goes where side effects are, and the checkpointer makes the pause durable.

options.text: Remove `issue_refund` from the agent and handle refunds by email
options.why: Safe, but it drops a core feature instead of controlling it.

explanation: Human-in-the-loop belongs on irreversible or sensitive actions. `interrupt_on` accepts `True`, `False` or a config with `allowed_decisions` (for example only approve and reject for refunds). Pair it with tracing in LangSmith to show the reviewers what each run did.

stem: A teammate asks when to use `create_agent`, Deep Agents or a hand-written LangGraph graph. Which statement matches LangChain's own positioning?

options.text: Deep Agents is a separate runtime that replaces LangGraph and does not use LangChain
options.why: Deep Agents builds on LangChain's agent and middleware, which run on LangGraph.

options.text: `create_agent` is a minimal harness of a model calling tools in a loop, customised with middleware; Deep Agents adds batteries such as a filesystem, subagents and skills; LangGraph suits flows that need more determinism than a standard loop
options.why: These are three composable layers: runtime (LangGraph), framework (LangChain), harness (Deep Agents).

options.text: Use LangGraph only for prototypes, because `create_agent` is required in production
options.why: LangGraph is the durable runtime underneath and is fully production-grade.

options.text: All three are interchangeable names for the same API
options.why: They sit at different levels of abstraction.

explanation: Agent equals model plus harness. LangChain's `create_agent` is an unopinionated harness. Deep Agents layers context-engineering defaults on top of it as middleware. A custom LangGraph graph is the right call when only part of a workflow is agentic, or the flow is not a simple loop.

stem: An `after_model` guardrail with `can_jump_to=["model"]` appends a correction message and jumps back to the model whenever the reply breaks a policy. In production, one request burns hundreds of model calls. What is the most robust fix?

options.text: Lower the model's temperature so it complies on the first retry
options.why: This reduces but does not bound retries; a stubborn case still loops.

options.text: Keep the guardrail, cap retries with a counter in middleware state or add `ModelCallLimitMiddleware`, and jump to `"end"` with a safe fallback reply when the cap is hit
options.why: A jump back to the model creates a loop, so it needs an explicit bound and a graceful exit.

options.text: Move the guardrail into `before_model`, so it runs before generation
options.why: It cannot judge a reply that does not exist yet.

options.text: Rely on the graph recursion limit to stop the loop
options.why: It does stop the loop eventually, but by raising an error after many wasted calls; it is a backstop, not a design.

explanation: Jumping to `model` from `after_model` is a valid self-correction pattern (a test showed the bad reply, the correction and then the good reply in state), but every such edge needs a bound. Track attempts in a custom state field (`state_schema` on the middleware), or add call-limit middleware, and end with a safe message.
